prompt: In Cunningham's metaphor, what is the interest on a technical debt?
hint: It is paid again and again, by whoever touches the code next.

choices.text: The work it would take to rework the code once
choices.why: That is the principal, paid once. Interest is what you pay for as long as you do not pay the principal.

choices.text: The extra cost added to every change that touches it
choices.why: Right: the longer change, the extra review, the workaround, the incident, for as long as the debt stays.

choices.text: The salary of the engineers who wrote the code
choices.why: What they cost when they wrote it is spent and gone; interest is what the code costs from now on.

choices.text: The production bugs it causes, counted at the end of each year
choices.why: Incidents are one part of the interest, not all of it; most of it is slower, harder changes that no bug count shows.

prompt: Why does Cunningham's version treat taking on debt as a good decision?
hint: What did his team learn by shipping?

choices.text: Debt costs nothing until the day it is repaid
choices.why: Interest is charged from the start on every change that touches the code; that is the danger he named.

choices.text: Finance prefers spending spread over several years
choices.why: The metaphor borrows finance's words, not its accounting; nobody spreads technical debt on purpose to suit a budget.

choices.text: A perfect design is out of reach anyway
choices.why: True, and not his argument. The point is that shipping is how you learn, and that the learning is then paid back into the code.

choices.text: Shipping early is how the team finds out what the right design is
choices.why: Right: the code reflects today's understanding, and shipping is what improves the understanding. The loan buys learning.

prompt: The work it would take to remove a debt, by reworking the code to match what the team now knows, is paid once. The lesson calls it the ___.
Coreto's admin screens for setting up a venue are badly designed, and they change very rarely. By the limits of the metaphor, what follows?

choices.text: They charge almost no interest, so repaying buys little
choices.why: Right: interest is paid only when somebody works in the code. Paying the principal here saves interest that was not being charged.

choices.text: They are the most urgent debt, being among the oldest
choices.why: Age is not cost. Debt that nobody touches charges nothing, however old it is.

choices.text: Their interest builds up quietly, as on a bank loan
choices.why: That is exactly where the metaphor misleads: a bank charges every month, and code charges only when it is changed.

choices.text: They are not debt at all, since the screens work
choices.why: Working code can still be debt if a better design can be named; this one simply charges little interest.

prompt: Where does the debt metaphor mislead, by the lesson? Choose all that apply.
hint: Compare code with a bank loan: who charges, who is told, who pays.

choices.text: Debt that nobody touches charges no interest
choices.why: Right: a bank charges every month; code charges only when somebody works in it.

choices.text: Borrowing is a bad decision for an engineering team
choices.why: The metaphor says the opposite, and the lesson agrees: a loan taken to learn faster is a good decision.

choices.text: Nobody sends a statement of what it cost
choices.why: Right: the interest is spread across hundreds of changes and nobody adds it up, which is why lesson 5 measures it.

choices.text: The person who borrowed is not the one who pays
choices.why: Right: the seat-hold code was written in Coreto's first years, and the Reservations team pays for it today.

choices.text: A loan can be repaid, and code cannot
choices.why: Code is repaid by reworking it to match what the team knows now; that is the principal.

prompt: Match each sentence from Fowler's quadrant to its box.
hint: Did the team know it was taking on debt? Did it know better?

pairs.left: "We must ship now and deal with consequences."
"Now we know how we should have done it."

prompt: The PDF ticket generator was a prudent loan taken before the first festival season. What turned it into a problem?
hint: Where did the note about replacing it end up?

choices.text: It was written carelessly by people who knew better
choices.why: That describes the flaky suite. The generator was a knowing shortcut with a plan to replace it.

choices.text: The festival season brought less revenue than the shortcut cost
choices.why: The lesson says the season paid for it many times over; the loan was sound.

choices.text: The library it replaced was the better design all along
choices.why: That library could not print the layouts festivals needed, which is why the loan was taken.

choices.text: It was never repaid
choices.why: Right: the season ended, the note stayed in a closed ticket, and a prudent loan became the case Cunningham warned about.

prompt: Which of these does the quadrant not tell you about a debt?

choices.text: Whether the team knew it was borrowing at the time
choices.why: That is the deliberate-or-inadvertent axis, one of the quadrant's two questions.

choices.text: How much it costs
choices.why: Right: a debt in any box can be cheap or ruinous. Lesson 5 prices it.

choices.text: What to change so that less of its kind is taken on
choices.why: That is what the box is for: each one calls for a different change.

choices.text: Whether the people who took it on could have done better
choices.why: That is the prudent-or-reckless axis, the other question.

prompt: Which change does the lesson attach to the box of Coreto's flaky end-to-end suite?
hint: Reckless and deliberate: what made the shortcut cheap?

choices.text: Write the loan down with a date for repayment
choices.why: That suits a prudent, deliberate loan with a plan behind it; the suite had no plan to honour.

choices.text: Accept it as the cost of learning
choices.why: Nothing was being learnt: the team knew why the tests failed and chose retries. That box is for the seat holds.

choices.text: A test that needs a retry to pass counts as failed
choices.why: Right: the reckless, deliberate box calls for changing the rule that made the shortcut cheap, and the retry was that rule.

choices.text: Pairing and training, since the team lacked the knowledge to write reliable tests
choices.why: Everybody involved knew how to write a reliable test; knowledge is the remedy for the inadvertent box.

prompt: A team stores uploads on a single server's disk, knowing it will need object storage once traffic outgrows one machine. They write that in the ticket, with the traffic level that triggers the move. Which box is this?
hint: Did they know, and did they plan?

choices.text: Reckless, deliberate: they knew a better design and skipped it
choices.why: Knowing a better design is not reckless when the shortcut comes with a trigger for repayment; that is a loan taken well.

choices.text: Prudent, deliberate
choices.why: Right: a knowing shortcut, written down with the condition for repaying it. What remains is to honour the trigger.

choices.text: Prudent, inadvertent: the right design will only show later
choices.why: They already know the better design and when they will need it, so nothing here is inadvertent.

choices.text: Not debt yet, since nothing has broken
choices.why: Debt is the gap between the design and the one they would choose for the load to come; it exists before anything breaks.

prompt: Which two questions does the lesson use to decide whether something is technical debt?
hint: One is about a design, the other about a cost.

choices.text: Is it old, and has its author left?
choices.why: Age and authorship describe history, not debt. Old code that nobody changes may cost nothing.

choices.text: Would you write it differently, and is it hard to read?
choices.why: That is preference. The test needs a better design you can name and a cost you can point at.

choices.text: Do you know a better design, and does each change cost something?
choices.why: Right: the first says there is something to repay, the second that there is interest to save by repaying it.

choices.text: Is it labelled as debt in the tracker, and is it on the roadmap?
choices.why: A label is where the long list comes from, and most of what sits under it is not debt.

prompt: "Checkout shows the wrong fee for half-price tickets" is on Coreto's debt list. Where does the lesson put it?
hint: Is the behaviour wrong, or the design?

choices.text: In the register, because the code around it is messy
choices.why: A messy surrounding does not turn a wrong behaviour into debt. Fixing it repays nothing.

choices.text: In the bug queue, fixed like any other bug
choices.why: Right: the behaviour is wrong. The bug is the commonest impostor, and it makes the debt list look longer than the debt is.

choices.text: Nowhere: half-price rules are the domain itself
choices.why: The rules are hard, but this is a wrong fee on a screen; it still has to be fixed.

choices.text: On the product roadmap, as a missing feature
choices.why: The feature exists and behaves wrongly; that is a bug, not product work nobody prioritised.

prompt: Changes to Coreto's pricing code are slow because half-price rules differ between states. Why does the lesson refuse to call that debt?
hint: Which of the two questions fails?

choices.text: The changes cost nothing
choices.why: They do cost something: every change is slow and needs care. The other question is the one that fails.

choices.text: Pricing belongs to product, so engineering cannot own its debt
choices.why: Ownership does not decide what is debt; a product area can carry engineering debt like any other.

choices.text: Nobody knows a design that would make the law simple
choices.why: Right: the difficulty belongs to the domain, and calling it debt sends a team looking for a refactoring that does not exist.

choices.text: The law changes, so any design would soon be out of date and need replacing
choices.why: Changing requirements are normal; the point is that no better design for them can be named today.

prompt: Of the four debts in Coreto's register, how many were taken on deliberately?
hint: Read the box column: prudent or reckless does not matter here.

prompt: Match each item from a debt list to where the lesson sends it.
hint: Only one of them is debt with interest, and it is not on the left.

pairs.left: A dependency past its supported life
Code in a style somebody dislikes

prompt: A search ranking was written by a contractor who did not know the team's search library could do it. Every ranking change now breaks something, and the team can describe a cleaner design. Which box, and does it go in the register?
hint: Did the author know there was a decision to make? Then apply the two questions.

choices.text: Reckless, deliberate; it goes in the register
choices.why: Deliberate means the author knew better and chose the shortcut; this author did not know the library existed.

choices.text: Prudent, inadvertent; it stays off the register
choices.why: Prudent, inadvertent debt is what a good team learns only by building; here the knowledge existed and was not sought.

choices.text: Reckless, inadvertent; it goes in the register
choices.why: Right: the author did not know there was a decision to make, and both questions answer yes: a nameable design and a cost on every change.

choices.text: None of the four: a contractor's code is a bug, not debt
choices.why: Who wrote it does not decide what it is. The behaviour works; the design charges interest.

prompt: Fowler's point about one box is that even an excellent team fills it, because understanding arrives after the code. The box is prudent and ___.
hint: "Now we know how we should have done it."

prompt: Line 6 of Coreto's first draft in lesson 1 read "Pay down technical debt". By this lesson, what does it lack?
hint: Could anybody prioritise it against a feature?

choices.text: Which debt, and what it costs each time
choices.why: Right: without a named debt and its interest, the phrase names a feeling, and a feeling cannot be weighed against a feature.

choices.text: A deadline for finishing it
choices.why: A date on an unnamed debt would still leave every team to decide which debt was meant.

choices.text: A budget line approved by the CFO
choices.why: Money comes after the register: Otávio can fund a named debt with a cost, not a phrase.

choices.text: The name of the team that took the debt on
choices.why: The quadrant judges decisions, not people; naming culprits stops the honest answers the register needs.

prompt: Put the steps from a long debt list to a register line in order.
hint: Find, test, classify, write; the price comes in lesson 5.
items: Follow the traces: slow changes, repeated incidents
Ask the two questions of each area
Classify the box with the people who were there
Write the row, with its cost in words and the evidence
Price it in hours a sprint
trap: Classifying before the two questions spends the conversation with the people who were there on items that are bugs or matters of taste.
